title: Kaushika's truth, and ahimsa first
hookLine: a truth that killed, and the limb that comes before the mat
carry: ahimsa first: tell the truth without the wound
tomorrow: can you stand up to someone without hating them?
last: HATHA: STAIRS TO A STILL MIND.

cards: A reply sits in the versions, every word true, every word built to sting. The Mahabharata has a story for that.
Arjuna, in a rage, draws his sword on his own brother Yudhishthira over an insult to his bow, and Krishna stops him with a tale. An ascetic named Kaushika had vowed always to tell the truth.
Robbers hunting some travelers asked him where they'd hidden. He told them, truthfully. The travelers were killed, and Krishna says that truth carried Kaushika not to heaven, but to hell.

teach.b: Krishna's point, as it's usually read: truth used to harm isn't dharma. The Yoga Sutras put the same order into a list.
Sutra 2.30 names the five yamas, the restraints: ahimsa, non-harming; satya, truthfulness; asteya, not stealing; brahmacharya, restraint of desire; aparigraha, not grasping.

In the eight limbs they come first, and ahimsa leads them. Then 2.31 makes them bigger than a class rule: kept everywhere, unbroken by birth, place, time or circumstance, they're called the great vow.

And 2.35, in paraphrase: when someone is firmly established in non-harming, hostility falls away in their presence. So ahimsa isn't only not hitting anyone. It reaches into words, and into the reply about to be sent.
It isn't being a doormat, either. Satya sits right beside it. Kaushika's failure wasn't speaking the truth; it was not caring what his truth would do.
A true thing can be said plainly without being made into a weapon. That's the part of yoga that traveled west more quietly. There's no pose for it.
But in the sutras it's the ground floor, and every other limb stands on it.

how: Teachers in the yoga tradition often begin with the yamas, the restraints, starting with ahimsa, as the ground of practice, following Yoga Sutras 2.30–2.35.

games.q: the ground floor. tap the pairs.
p: unbroken by birth, place or time

s: in the Mahabharata, Kaushika is praised for telling the robbers the truth
Krishna tells it as a warning: a truth that led to killing fell short of dharma.
in the sutras, the five restraints come before posture
they're the first of the eight limbs, with ahimsa first.
non-harming means never saying a hard truth
satya, truthfulness, sits right beside it.

games.q: a coworker takes credit for your idea in a meeting. which reply fits the yamas?
o: 'actually, that was mine,' with a cutting joke so it lands.
say plainly that it was your idea, and leave out the jab.
say nothing; non-harming means letting it go.
games.why: ahimsa and satya sit side by side: say the true thing, plainly, without making it a weapon. Kaushika's truth harmed; yours doesn't have to.

practice: Bring to mind one person you're at odds with right now. Name, silently, what you want from the situation; then the part of you that wants to sting back; then one plain, true sentence you could say that doesn't wound.
Give each a few slow breaths.

wordCard.voice: Yoga's journey west: today, the part that traveled quietly: five restraints, with ahimsa, non-harming, first.
